title: Pain and Laughter
html:
First, we cry. Then, we laugh.

Why, though, when our pains accumulate and our tears crest over our weathered faces, are we compelled to make light of them?

In the changing seasons of life, one has no choice but to confront bad weather. If you live long enough, you can be sure that, one day, you’ll be caught in a storm so turbulent you’ll wonder if you’ll ever see the sun again.

But all storms, just as they emerged from nothingness, will return to nothingness.

“This too shall pass,” we remind ourselves.

As the skies clear and the birds begin to sing again, we’re left cold and broken—a sopping mess of fear and sadness, mustering up the strength to see the beauty in the world again.

How, though, can we rekindle the levity with which we skipped down the sidewalks as children? How, when we have come to know such pain, can we heal?

There exists a realm where all tragedies are held, with care and understanding, so they can molt into founts of solace and consolation. This is the realm of comedy.

When tragedies become the subjects of humor, we experience them differently. In the moment, tragedies are just that: tragic. “This is terrible. This is horrible. This is cruel,” we say. And we’re right. But, with time, if we offer up our troubles to comedy, we’re allowed to say, “That was terrible. That was horrible. That was cruel. And that is okay.” To joke about our pains is to begin to accept them, but if we do not accept them, they will destroy us.

There is enough darkness in this world to cast shadows over all of us, but a readiness to laugh—to cast light into the darkness—ensures that we’ll always see a way forward.

We laugh because we’re in pain.

We’re in pain because we’re alive.
